name: Coloring (contrast / complexion) maxxing

lead: Coloring maxxing treats the face as a set of light and dark elements: iris against sclera, brows and lashes against skin, teeth against lips, hair against complexion. The idea is that clearer, more distinct contrasts make the face look alert, healthy and defined, and that people can adjust them through grooming, skincare, dyeing, makeup and clothing.

There is real research behind part of this. Perception studies by Richard Russell and colleagues found that luminance contrast between facial features and surrounding skin differs between men and women, and that makeup raises it in female faces. Forum guides go further, with colour typologies and rules of thumb that have not been tested.

paras: Common routes in forum guides include whitening teeth, reducing eye redness and dullness for brighter sclera, shaping or tinting brows and lashes, evening skin tone and treating dark circles, choosing a hair colour relative to eye and skin colour, and picking clothing colours that contrast with or flatter the complexion. Many of these are cosmetic or grooming steps that show results as soon as they are applied.

Most coloring steps are low-risk grooming, but individual methods carry their own risks, such as irritation from bleaching or dye products and sun damage from tanning. Opinions differ in the community on whether high contrast suits men; one thread argues contrast is overrated for male faces.

angle.text: Coloring maxxing changes how the face reads through tone and colour, using grooming, skincare, makeup, hair colour and clothing. Practitioners report that the effects show up in photos and in person quickly.

lead: Coloring maxxing (also coloringmaxxing, the coloring guide or the coloring pill) is a looksmaxxing framework about how the colours and tonal contrasts of a face combine into an overall impression. Its central claim is that well-defined contrast between the eyes, brows, lashes, teeth, lips, skin and hair makes a face look sharper, more alert and healthier, while low contrast makes even well-structured features look soft or flat [1].

People who follow it improve their appearance through colour and tone rather than bone structure: brighter teeth and sclera, even skin, defined brows and lashes, a considered hair colour and clothing that complements the complexion [1][2]. Because many of these steps are grooming or cosmetic, forum members often describe them as among the fastest changes available, visible in photos and in person as soon as they are made.

Part of the idea rests on published perception research. Richard Russell, Aurélie Porcheron and colleagues have measured luminance and colour contrast between facial features and the surrounding skin and reported that higher contrast is associated with faces being perceived as healthier and younger, and that cosmetics raise it [3][4]. The framework also overlaps with seasonal colour analysis, a fashion and styling tradition that became a social-media trend in the 2020s [5]. Forum guides add their own typologies and rules of thumb, such as hair darker than the eyes counting as good contrast, which have not been formally tested [6][2].

paras: The framework looks at the face as an arrangement of light and dark regions. A widely shared forum guide describes facial contrast as the differences between the light and dark elements of the face and lists the eyes, teeth, eyebrows, hair and skin as the contributors [1]. It says clear sclera make the iris stand out and give a more alert look, while dull or darkened sclera make the face look tired [1].

A longer community guide titled the coloring guide covers why coloring matters, principles of ideal coloring, colouring types with the colours said to suit each, and ways to improve coloring [2]. Other threads concentrate on narrower topics: eyebrow and eyelash colouring [7], white teeth and sclera as a quick contrast gain [8], skin complexion [9], choosing a BB cream shade for face colour [10], and using clothing to create contrast [11].

In practice the word covers two overlapping ideas. One is contrast: how strongly the eyes, brows, lips and hair stand out against the skin. The other is colour harmony or complexion: skin tone and evenness, undertone, and which hair and clothing colours sit well with them. Forum guides move between the two, and the research literature mostly addresses the first.

The term circulates mainly on looksmax.org, where guides by members have been revised over time; the author of one popular guide says it is a remastered version of an earlier thread and calls the first attempt incomplete [2]. That guide, credited to the member enchanted_elixir, lays out its structure as an introduction, the importance of coloring, principles of ideal coloring, coloring types and ways to improve coloring [2]. A teaser thread for coloringmaxxing dates to 2020, and later threads claim coloring and hair account for a large share of how a person looks [12][13]. Contrast-focused guides continued to appear into 2025 [6][1].

Outside the forum, the vocabulary sits next to the much larger consumer interest in personal colour analysis. Wikipedia's account notes that the practice peaked in the early 1980s, returned in the 2010s through image and colour consultants, and went viral on social media, especially TikTok, in the 2020s, with the New York Times covering the trend in 2024 [5]. Looksmaxxing guides draw on the same intuition that colours can be matched to a person, while adding the facial-contrast language of perception research.

Members commonly state that a hair colour darker than the eyes is a good rule of thumb for contrast, and one thread contrasts examples of faces said to have high and low contrast [6]. Guides argue that bright sclera and white teeth are the easiest contrast gains and are quick to change [8][1]. Some posters argue that fair skin is the most preferred complexion by women [14]. Other members dispute the weight put on contrast: one thread argues that contrast is a poor strategy for men and questions why it is promoted [15].

Described in general terms, forum guides group actions into teeth whitening, eye brightening, brow and lash shaping or tinting, skin evenness and tone, hair colour and clothing choices [1][7][8][11]. Skin-focused threads cover complexion and shade-matching of base products [9][10][16].

Makeup is one of the most direct ways to change contrast, and the research below suggests why it is so effective on photographs and in person. Hair dye, brow tinting and clothing choices change contrast without altering the face itself, so members treat them as reversible experiments [7][11].

Researchers at Bangor and Swansea examined facial contrast in a large set of faces and reported that women have higher eye contrast and lower brow contrast than men, that cosmetics amplify these sex-linked contrasts, and that makeup also boosts contrasts that fade with age [3]. The paper, by Jones, Russell and Ward, appeared in Evolutionary Psychology in 2015 [3].

A 2016 study by Russell and colleagues measured contrast in a large sample of Caucasian women's faces and related it to health ratings; most contrast measures were positively associated with perceived health, and in two follow-up experiments faces with digitally increased contrast were rated healthier than those with decreased contrast [4]. A 2017 study by Porcheron and colleagues measured contrast in photographs of Chinese, Latin American and Black South African women aged 20 to 80, found that most contrast measures declined with age across groups, and reported that French and Chinese participants rated faces younger when age-related contrast was raised and older when it was lowered; the authors suggested this may help explain why cosmetics make faces look younger [4]. A 2019 study by Russell and colleagues found that makeup made 40- and 50-year-old women look younger, had no effect on 30-year-olds and made 20-year-olds look older, which they linked to youth cues such as skin homogeneity and facial contrast [4].

Earlier work by Russell reported that increasing the contrast of eyes and mouth raised attractiveness ratings for female faces but lowered them for male faces, a finding the forum debate about men and contrast echoes [15][3]. These studies used mostly female faces, and none tested forum rules of thumb such as hair-versus-eye darkness.

Seasonal color analysis is the styling tradition of matching clothing and makeup colours to skin, hair and eye colouring [5]. Wikipedia traces it to nineteenth-century colour theory: Michel Eugène Chevreul's 1839 The Laws of Contrast of Colour, Albert Munsell's hue, value and chroma system, and Johannes Itten's 1961 The Art of Color, which linked personal colours to the four seasons [5]. Robert Dorr's Color Key System of the 1950s divided complexions into cool and warm keys, and Suzanne Caygill's 1980 Color: The Essence of You created sub-types within each season [5]. Popular books such as Bernice Kentner's Color Me a Season (1978), Carole Jackson's Color Me Beautiful (1980) and Color Wonderful (1986) spread the four-season model [5].

Systems are organised in several ways: by season, by warm versus cool, by contrast level, or by undertone [5]. A 2007 study by Tracy Cassidy found that several systems claiming to use hue, saturation and value often relied on only two of them, and critics note that no standard credential is needed to work as a colour analyst [5]. Wikipedia also reports a 2021 study by David Perrett and Reiner Sprengelmeyer that found consistent clothing-colour preferences for fair and tanned skin in White women, though without validating the traditional seasonal categories [5]. The contrast-based variants of colour analysis are the closest relative of the looksmaxxing coloring guides.

Most coloring steps are low-risk grooming, but individual methods carry their own risks, such as irritation from bleaching or dye products near the eyes and sun damage from tanning. Community disagreement is mostly about relevance: whether high contrast suits men, and whether guides that sort people into colour types describe real differences [15][2]. Discussion of complexion sometimes turns to skin colour and ethnicity, where posts reflect strong and varied views [14].
No studies found on coloring maxxing as a framework. Related perception research on facial contrast, cosmetics and perceived health and age is described above [3][4].
